title: Strings From Two Block Sizes
statement:
You build a binary string starting from the empty string. Each step appends one block: either zero copies of the character "0", or one copies of the character "1". You may stop after any step.

Count the different strings you can build whose length is between low and high, both included. The count can be huge, so return it modulo 1 000 000 007.

examples.why: Length 2: "00", "11". Length 3: "000", "011", "110". The single "0" has length 1 and does not count.
"0000", "00111" and "11100". The order of the blocks matters, so "00"+"111" and "111"+"00" are different strings.
Every block has length 2, so every string has an even length. Length 3 is impossible.

hints: Forget the range for a moment. How many strings of exactly length L can you build?
Look at the last block. A string of length L ends with a block of zeros (the rest has length L − zero) or a block of ones (the rest has length L − one). Different last blocks give different strings.
ways[L] = ways[L − zero] + ways[L − one], with ways[0] = 1. Fill it from 1 to high and add up ways[low..high], all modulo 1 000 000 007.

explain.intuition:
This is the staircase problem in disguise: each step climbs either zero or one stairs, and a string is one route up. Two different routes always give different strings, because the first block where they differ starts with a different character.

So count routes by their last step. Every string of length L is a shorter string plus one final block, which means ways[L] = ways[L − zero] + ways[L − one]. Compute this for every length up to high and sum the lengths you care about.
steps: Make ways of length high + 1 filled with 0 and set ways[0] = 1 (the empty string).
For L from 1 to high: add ways[L − zero] if L ≥ zero, add ways[L − one] if L ≥ one, and take the result modulo 1 000 000 007.
Sum ways[L] for L from low to high, again modulo 1 000 000 007.
pitfalls: Counting only strings of length exactly high. Every length in the range counts.
Forgetting the modulo on the final sum. Each ways[L] is reduced, but adding up to 100 000 of them is not.
Treating zero == one as one choice. A block of zeros and a block of ones of the same length are still different strings.

solutions.title: Count block mixes with binomials
solutions.idea: Pick how many zero-blocks a and one-blocks b to use. If a·zero + b·one is in range, those blocks can be ordered in C(a + b, a) ways. Pascal's triangle gives the binomials without overflow.

solutions.title: DP on the last block
solutions.idea: ways[L] = ways[L − zero] + ways[L − one]. Sum the lengths in [low, high].

solutions.title: Push counts forward
solutions.idea: Same table, filled the other way: every reachable length passes its count on to length + zero and length + one.

followups: There are k block types instead of two, each with its own length and character. What is the new recurrence and its cost?
Only the last max(zero, one) entries of the table are ever read. Rewrite it with a ring buffer of that size.
